justification: Carrying span: “in the cold the first blow took the cone two-thirds as deep, and the count nearly doubled” — cold grid = shallower first blow, higher blow count. A dies on “how many blows take it to a hundred millimetres” (the count stops at 100 mm; the bed is “130 millimetres”, so the cone was never driven to the bottom). B dies on “under a ring weight raised to a collar and let fall” — the collar fixes the drop height, so it is not “from whatever height each point seemed to need”. D is the exact inversion of “The gap between my February morning and my July afternoon is still wider than the gap between this school and any other school I test.”

Carrying span: “In the top 50 millimetres the fibre came out at about 8 per cent by weight; lower down it was nearer 3.” A dies on “the wax he brought up from the bottom was in better condition than the wax at the top”. B dies on “the grains he sieved came out much as the original specification had them”. C dies on “Eighty millimetres of it had not been turned since the day it was laid, and under nine years of hoofprints it had gone firm enough to lean a spade on” — below the tines the bed was hard, not loose, and the hoofprints reached it.

Carrying span: “In the schools laid on plain sand and fibre and kept damp with a sprinkler, the morning grid and the afternoon grid sit almost on top of one another. The waxed ones move, whatever their age”, with the mechanism given as “The wax is a paraffin blend, and it is doing most of that work.” Absence of wax is the stated difference. A dies on “whatever their age” plus “some of them older than this one” — age is explicitly ruled out. C dies on “plain sand and fibre” — these schools have no wax at all. D dies on “the morning grid and the afternoon grid” — the same two hours are read, not different ones.

Carrying span: “Here Pallenmoor is careful, and the care is the most useful thing about him”, where the care is exactly the limiting of his own figures (“I can’t put a number on it; these readings won’t carry one”; “The tester measures a surface; there is no horse above the cone”; “he would argue it from the veterinary literature rather than from his own figures”). B dies on that same soundness paragraph: the yard’s later tine change and un-ordered heaters are reported flatly and the soundness question is left standing — “The tester measures a surface; there is no horse above the cone.” C dies on “Both figures moved, and they moved together” — the penetrometer corroborates the riders rather than explaining them away. D dies on “That is a good deal less than the trade’s brochures offer, and it is worth more than they are.”

Carrying spans: temperature — “Below about six degrees the coating is stiff … Above about twenty-five it goes slack … and the floor gets deep”; tine depth — “The leveller’s tines were set to 50 millimetres. The bed is 130 … the machine had been slowly sorting the bed into a loose layer riding on a hard one”, with the fix being “The tines have been dropped to 80 millimetres … to bring the pan up.” Both govern how it rides. A dies on “the wax he brought up from the bottom was in better condition than the wax at the top” — the unturned layer is not being worn out. B was weighed and dies on “Above about twenty-five it goes slack” plus “The heaters have been costed and not ordered”: warming a February school does not reproduce a July afternoon that may sit past the slack threshold, and the text offers no heated-school reading. D is the inversion of “The temperature is doing more in that room than the tractor is.”

Carrying span: the clause pairs two unsignalled unanimities — “two hundred people find the same half-second” and “the ending is unanimous … again there has been no signal” — so the connective must add a parallel case; “Equally” does that. A (“Hence”) fails because a unanimous ending is not caused by a unanimous start; the text presents them as two instances of the same puzzle, not as premise and consequence. B (“Rather”) needs a correction of what precedes, but nothing is being corrected — “again” marks repetition, not contrast. D (“Elsewhere”) needs a change of place, yet both events happen in the one “school hall”.

Carrying span: “The risk of putting your hands together in a quiet room is that the room may not ___ in, and for the length of one clap you are alone” — the feared outcome is that nobody else joins in, and “join in” is the phrasal verb for adding one’s hands to another’s, confirmed by “that is why the second pair of hands matters more than the first”. B (“cut in”) and D (“break in”) both mean to interrupt, which reverses the risk — being interrupted is not what leaves you “alone with an opinion nobody asked for”. C (“fall in”) means to take up formation and needs “with” to mean agreement, so it does not license the bare “the room may not fall in”.

Carrying span: “the coming-down is a ___ about how long is decent, conducted at speed and without words” — a process, still under way, in which the hall converges on an acceptable duration; “negotiation” takes both “about” and “conducted”. A (“transaction”) names an exchange of goods or money, not a wordless working-out of “how long is decent”. C (“bargain”) is the struck agreement — one strikes a bargain rather than conducting one at speed. D (“settlement”) is likewise the outcome, which contradicts “the coming-down” being the thing described as ongoing.

Carrying span: “Although what a hall gives an eight-year-old is ___, it is not permitted to run long” — “Although” demands a property that would argue for length, and “wholehearted” supplies it against the cap of “Four or five seconds”. C (“brief”) points the same way as “not permitted to run long”, so the concession collapses. A (“rehearsed”) contradicts the paragraph’s premise, “No one has agreed to anything, there is no conductor to watch”, and yields no concession either. B (“outspoken”) is a property of speech, whereas this exchange is expressly “conducted at speed and without words”.

Carrying span: “A room asked for a big hand for a stranger will give one ___, and everybody present can hear that it is not the same sound the recorder player got” — solicited applause, audibly lesser, is given out of obligation: “dutifully”. C (“instinctively”) is killed by “asked for”, which is the opposite of instinct, and by the whole paragraph heading “The mechanism shows itself when it slips”. D (“eagerly”) would make the sound warmer, contradicting “it is not the same sound the recorder player got”, that sound being the spontaneous one from the opening. A (“narrowly”) has no reading here — applause is not given by a narrow margin or in a narrow manner.

Carrying span: “Between stations the shocks were tiny. ‘It’s the stop at the far end that does it’” — the damage happens on arrival, which is why the fix was foam in the bins. A dies on “The loop runs at the speed it always has” — rejects fell because “Two bins are lined with foam”, not from slowing. B dies on “Nothing shows on the ward; the colour comes with the spinning.” C dies on “Blood gases have never gone by tube; a porter walks those down.”

The two landmark pairs name one span. The claim runs “from the stone gap down to the lane”; the survey ran “along the bank, from the ash to the culvert”; and the passage supplies the identity in advance — “An ash grew in the stone gap; a culvert ran under the lane.” Ash = stone gap, culvert = lane, both “along the bank”, so Ruddiforth claimed exactly the pegged ground, a month after the pegging, which is what the piece implies about the quarrel (confirmed by “In February Ruddiforth offered to leave the timber and keep the ground” and by the quarrel ending once “The scheme was given up … no land was taken” and “In 1851 both farms laid the thorn together”). A dies on “The neighbour’s attorney enclosed a tracing of the railway company’s deposited plan” — the other side, not Ruddiforth’s. C is inverted: the claim is “In November 1845” and the survey “The previous October a surveyor had chained and pegged”, the past perfect and the date both placing it before the letters. B dies on “cut from above by one and cleaned from below by the other” plus “both sides agree the thorn was last laid in 1839” — the hedge was tended and its laying was not in contention.

Bärande spån: “Ändå ska den bäras. Från och med nästa spelår bör texten gå på varje föreställning på stora scenen, inte på fyra utvalda”, medan hon samtidigt erkänner kostnaden i spelet: “Textremsan låser repliken … den som vet att remsan går spelar inte som förut. Så lyder ensemblens invändning, och jag skriver under på den.” B är rak motsats till “Ett svepskäl är det inte.” C faller på “Fler särskilda kvällar begär jag inte. Fyra kan bli sex och sedan åtta” samt “Att ensemblen vänjer sig vid remsan kan jag inte lova.” D faller på “Om lilla scenen kan bära samma sak vet jag inte … och något förslag för den scenen har jag inte.”

Bärande spån: “I länsteaterns höstprogram har de textade föreställningarna en egen rad, inklämd mellan syntolkning och skolföreställningar.” A faller på “Raden rymmer fyra kvällar” — åtta förekommer bara i det avvisade hypotetiska “Fyra kan bli sex och sedan åtta”. B flyttar över en annan sak i programbladet: det är “Slingans symbol” som “finns längst ned på varje uppslag”, inte raden. C flyttar likaså: namnet på den som sköter tekniken står “Längre bak i programbladet … under rubriken Text och teknik”, alltså inte på raden.

Bärande spån: “Skaren som bar en karl gick sönder under hoven” — samma skare som bär en människa brister under hoven, med förklaringen “En hov samlar hela djurets tyngd på en yta stor som en tallrik”. B faller på samma mening: “mot det hjälper varken broddar eller lättare lass.” C faller på “Lassen gick på kälke i stället, och kälken drogs för hand. Skidor dög till att ta sig fram med, men inte till att dra med” — skidorna ersatte inte dragandet. D faller på “Skaren är inte hal om morgonen. Den är sträv som fint grus under sulan, och blank blir den först fram på dagen”, och hästarna var då ändå kvar i stallet.

Bärande spån: “Veckorna kom när de kom … Somliga år blev det fyra morgnar på hela vintern, och ett par vintrar uteblev skaren. Man såg på himlen och bestämde sig kvällen innan.” A faller på nästa mening: “Var gård körde för sig, och sällan väntade någon in grannen.” C faller på “Man ger sig i väg vid fyra, i mörker, och vid tio är det över” samt “Ett lass som inte är hemma vid tio blir liggande till nästa natt” — arbetet löpte över flera morgnar, inte en enda lång natt. D faller på “Vi gick tvärs över sjön mot Olivia Sjödins lada, en väg som inte finns resten av året” och “räknas varken diken eller gärdsgårdar”.

Carrier: 'in the cold the first blow took the cone two-thirds as deep, and the count nearly doubled' — cold grid = shallower first blow + higher count, exactly C. A dies on 'how many blows take it to a hundred millimetres' against 'The floor is 130 millimetres' — he never drives to the bottom of the bed. B dies on 'under a ring weight raised to a collar and let fall' — the collar fixes the drop height; nothing is set by eye per point. D inverts the text: 'The gap between my February morning and my July afternoon is still wider than the gap between this school and any other school I test' puts the between-visit spread wider, not the between-arena spread.

Carrier: 'In the top 50 millimetres the fibre came out at about 8 per cent by weight; lower down it was nearer 3' — much less fibre at the bottom than the top. A dies on 'the wax he brought up from the bottom was in better condition than the wax at the top'. B dies on 'The sand itself had hardly changed: the grains he sieved came out much as the original specification had them'. C dies on 'Eighty millimetres of it had not been turned since the day it was laid, and under nine years of hoofprints it had gone firm enough to lean a spade on' — the untouched lower bed is hard, not loose.

Carrier: 'In the schools laid on plain sand and fibre and kept damp with a sprinkler, the morning grid and the afternoon grid sit almost on top of one another. The waxed ones move, whatever their age.' The contrast pair isolates the absence of wax as what keeps them steady across the day. A dies on 'whatever their age' plus 'some of them older than this one' — age is explicitly ruled out. C dies on 'laid on plain sand and fibre' — they carry no wax at all. D dies on 'the same pair of grids' / 'the morning grid and the afternoon grid' — the sprinkler schools are read on the same two-grid protocol, not at some other hour.

Carrier: 'Here Pallenmoor is careful, and the care is the most useful thing about him', with the care spelled out as the limits he sets — 'The tester measures a surface; there is no horse above the cone' and 'I can't put a number on it; these readings won't carry one' — and closed by 'it is worth more than they are'. That is the writer taking his self-imposed limits to be his real contribution. B dies because the yard's later moves are reported as tines dropped to 80 mm and heaters 'costed and not ordered' — nothing in the text reads them as answering 'whether any of this keeps a horse sound'. C dies because the riders are vindicated, not psychologised: 'Both figures moved, and they moved together'. D dies on 'That is a good deal less than the trade's brochures offer, and it is worth more than they are' — the brochures are rated below his figures, not as a supplement to them.

Carrier: the two established drivers of how the floor rides are the room temperature — 'The temperature is doing more in that room than the tractor is', 'Below about six degrees the coating is stiff... Above about twenty-five it goes slack' — and the tine setting — 'The leveller's tines were set to 50 millimetres. The bed is 130... the machine had been slowly sorting the bed into a loose layer riding on a hard one'. A dies on 'the wax he brought up from the bottom was in better condition than the wax at the top' — the unturned lower bed shows no cold-driven wear. B overreaches: the heaters were 'costed and not ordered', the warm grid was read at eighteen degrees while slackening starts 'above about twenty-five', so no February-equals-July conclusion is available. D directly contradicts 'The temperature is doing more in that room than the tractor is'.

Gap (1) joins two matched observations: the start is unanimous with 'no conductor to watch', and '___, the ending is unanimous... and again there has been no signal'. 'again' marks a parallel, so an additive/likewise adverb is required: 'Equally'. 'Hence' fails because the ending is not caused by the opening. 'Rather' fails because nothing in the second clause corrects or replaces the first. 'Elsewhere' is spatial and has no place to point to — the whole scene is one hall.

Gap (2): 'the room may not ___ in, and for the length of one clap you are alone' requires the phrasal verb for others adding their applause: 'join in'. The next sentence confirms it — 'the second pair of hands matters more than the first'. 'cut in' means to interrupt, wrong direction. 'fall in' means to form up in line. 'break in' means to interrupt or intrude. None yields 'the room may not add its clapping to yours'.

Gap (3): 'the coming-down is a ___ about how long is decent, conducted at speed and without words'. Both 'about <an open question>' and the verb 'conducted' select an ongoing process noun: 'negotiation'. 'transaction' is an exchange of goods or money, not something held 'about how long is decent'. 'bargain' and 'settlement' both name the outcome reached, not the process 'conducted at speed' — and the paragraph's point is the unresolved, in-flight adjusting ('the sound comes down faster than it went up').

Gap (4) sits under 'Although' and must contrast with 'it is not permitted to run long' — i.e. the applause is genuine and generous yet still capped at 'Four or five seconds'. 'wholehearted' supplies that tension, and is confirmed downstream by 'it is not the same sound the recorder player got', which presupposes the child got the warm one. 'brief' destroys the concession — 'Although it is brief, it is not permitted to run long' is a tautology, not a contrast. 'rehearsed' contradicts the essay's premise: 'No one has agreed to anything'. 'outspoken' is a property of speech, not of applause, and creates no contrast with length.

Gap (5): 'A room asked for a big hand for a stranger will give one ___, and everybody present can hear that it is not the same sound the recorder player got' — the applause is produced on request and is audibly hollow, so 'dutifully'. 'instinctively' contradicts 'asked for' — this clapping is prompted, not spontaneous — and would imply genuineness. 'eagerly' contradicts 'not the same sound'. 'narrowly' has no reading here: it means barely or by a small margin, and nothing in the sentence is being measured or scraped through.

Carrier: 'Between stations the shocks were tiny. “It’s the stop at the far end that does it”' — the damage happens at arrival, which is D. A dies on 'The loop runs at the speed it always has' — the halving of rejects came from 'Two bins are lined with foam', not from slowing. B dies on 'Nothing shows on the ward; the colour comes with the spinning'. C dies on 'Blood gases have never gone by tube; a porter walks those down'.

The text pegs each landmark to the other member of its pair: 'An ash grew in the stone gap; a culvert ran under the lane.' The claim runs 'from the stone gap down to the lane'; the surveyor 'chained and pegged the line along the bank, from the ash to the culvert'. Ash = stone gap and culvert = lane, so the two stretches coincide — the claimed ground is the pegged ground, which is D, and it is what makes 'In February Ruddiforth offered to leave the timber and keep the ground' legible. A dies on 'The neighbour’s attorney enclosed a tracing of the railway company’s deposited plan' — the other side put the plan in, not Ruddiforth’s attorney. B dies on 'Until 1845 the hedge had never been in dispute' plus 'cut from above by one and cleaned from below by the other' — the bank was tended, and 'both sides agree the thorn was last laid in 1839' is offered as common ground, not as a grievance. C reverses the chronology: the claim is 'In November 1845', and the pegging is 'The previous October a surveyor had chained and pegged the line' — pluperfect, October 1845, before the letters begin.

Bärande sats: 'Från och med nästa spelår bör texten gå på varje föreställning på stora scenen, inte på fyra utvalda', och skribenten medger kostnaden: 'Textremsan låser repliken... Så lyder ensemblens invändning, och jag skriver under på den... Ändå ska den bäras.' Det är precis A:s två led. B motsägs ordagrant av 'Ett svepskäl är det inte'. C motsägs av 'Fler särskilda kvällar begär jag inte' och av 'Att ensemblen vänjer sig vid remsan kan jag inte lova'. D motsägs av 'Om lilla scenen kan bära samma sak vet jag inte... något förslag för den scenen har jag inte'.

Bärande sats: 'har de textade föreställningarna en egen rad, inklämd mellan syntolkning och skolföreställningar' — exakt D. A motsägs av 'Raden rymmer fyra kvällar'; 'åtta' förekommer bara i den hypotetiska trappan 'Fyra kan bli sex och sedan åtta'. B flyttar över ett drag från hörselslingan: 'Slingans symbol finns längst ned på varje uppslag i programbladet'. C flyttar över ett drag från en annan del av bladet: 'Längre bak i programbladet står Ingegerd Hörnfeldt under rubriken Text och teknik' — inte på raden.

Bärande sats: 'Skaren som bar en karl gick sönder under hoven' — hovarna sjönk igenom där folk bar, alltså A, med förklaringen 'En hov samlar hela djurets tyngd på en yta stor som en tallrik'. B motsägs av 'mot det hjälper varken broddar eller lättare lass'. C motsägs av 'Lassen gick på kälke i stället, och kälken drogs för hand. Skidor dög till att ta sig fram med, men inte till att dra med'. D motsägs av 'Skaren är inte hal om morgonen... och blank blir den först fram på dagen' — färderna gjordes på morgonen.

Bärande sats: 'Veckorna kom när de kom... Somliga år blev det fyra morgnar på hela vintern, och ett par vintrar uteblev skaren. Man såg på himlen och bestämde sig kvällen innan' — dagarna gick inte att bestämma i förväg, alltså B. A motsägs av 'Var gård körde för sig, och sällan väntade någon in grannen'. C motsägs av 'Bärigheten varar några timmar. Man ger sig i väg vid fyra, i mörker, och vid tio är det över' — korta morgnar, inte en lång natt. D motsägs av 'Vi gick tvärs över sjön mot Olivia Sjödins lada, en väg som inte finns resten av året'.
